_comment: Drafted replies keyed by tweet id. Edit freely; the review page reads these as starting text and sends whatever is in the box.

replies.2039527567204704560: Ferrofluid separation is genuinely clever. The bar it has to clear is that reverse osmosis already removes microplastics along with PFAS, lead and fluoride, so the interesting question is cost and throughput rather than capability.
replies.2029338367943688702: Polyester is plastic, and the shedding is the part that gets missed. Synthetic clothing sheds hundreds of thousands of microplastic fibres every wash, and they end up in indoor air and house dust as much as in waterways.
replies.2060403042084933833: That framing is closer than most. The study tested one isolated strain, Leuconostoc mesenteroides CBA3656, in germ free mice, not kimchi the food. It bound about 87 percent of polystyrene nanoplastics in a dish. Two very different claims.
replies.2060152157739913412: Worth one caveat: that study tested a single isolated strain, Leuconostoc mesenteroides CBA3656, in germ free mice, not kimchi the food. It bound about 87 percent of polystyrene nanoplastics in a dish, which is a long way from eating kimchi.
replies.2033255150152794289: Billions per cup, and the fix is unusually cheap. Loose leaf with a steel infuser takes plastic out of the brewing path entirely, no special product required.
replies.2034572325039792277: The base is usually polyvinyl acetate, the same polymer family as white glue. What makes it hard to avoid is that the whole thing hides behind one ingredient line reading gum base. Chicle based brands are the way around it.
replies.2003215719987589611: Tire wear is one of the largest single sources and gets almost no regulatory attention, which is the strange part. It also shows up in roadside air and household dust, not only in waterways.
replies.1744799330241048854: That 240,000 figure is what moved this from niche to mainstream. The detail worth keeping is that most of them were nanoplastics, which is both the fraction small enough to cross into tissue and the fraction most filters are never tested against.
replies.1894146042473357355: Reverse osmosis is the right call. It is the only household technology that removes PFAS, microplastics, lead and fluoride together. Everything else covers a subset, which is fine once you know which subset you actually need.
replies.2061886419828678853: No human study shows fibre removes plastic particles already in your tissues. The kernel of truth is narrower: some fibre research shows lower BPA, which is a chemical rather than a particle. That swap is the most common trick in this whole category.
replies.1995176669749919806: Microwave safe is a melting standard, not a health one. It means the container will not deform. Borosilicate and tempered soda lime glass are both genuinely microwave safe and sidestep the question entirely.
replies.1920131611112427935: The size distinction matters more than most coverage admits. Nanoplastics are the fraction that crosses membranes, and certification has not caught up to them. NSF 401 covers microplastics, with no equivalent for nano.
replies.2025564201230504065: Fleece is a particularly bad case because the pile is cut fibre, so there are many more loose ends to shed. Synthetics release hundreds of thousands of fibres per wash. Washing cold and less often measurably reduces it.
